meta.description: An English proverb, not an Erasmus quotation. The earliest documented English wording is in Thomas Adams's 1630 sermons; the idea itself is far older.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Prevention is better than cure'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote sites pin it on Erasmus with no source. It's actually an old English proverb, first documented in Thomas Adams's sermons (1630).

answer.label: Not Erasmus — an old English proverb
answer.authorDates: Proverbial · documented in English since the early 1600s
answer.sourceLine: Widely printed under Erasmus’s name, but this five-word English proverb appears in none of his (Latin) writings. It is a proverbial saying: the earliest documented English form is in the sermons of the clergyman Thomas Adams (1630), and the modern wording spread in the 1800s. The underlying idea — meet trouble before it grows — is ancient.

source.excerpt: Prevention is so much better than healing, because it saves the labour of being sick.
trail: Quote databases from Quotefancy ↗ to BrainyQuote print the line under Erasmus’s name — every one of them without a book, page, or date.
The scholarly quote-tracer WIST ↗ lists it under Erasmus only as “(Attributed)” — its label for a line with no located source.
The Phrase Finder ↗ traces the earliest English form to the sermons of Thomas Adams (Works, 1630) and the modern wording’s spread to T. C. Haliburton’s “The Clockmaker” (1837).
A two-thousand-year history ↗ of the idea runs from Chinese medicine and the Roman poet Persius (c. AD 58) to Franklin’s “an ounce of prevention” (1736).
source.excerptNote: The earliest documented English wording of the proverb — Thomas Adams’s phrasing, not the trimmed modern five-word version, and not Erasmus.

author.name: Thomas Adams
author.heading: Thomas Adams
author.bio: Thomas Adams (1583–1652) was an English clergyman and preacher, sometimes called ‘the prose Shakespeare of the Puritans’ for his vivid style. The earliest known English formulation of this proverb — ‘prevention is so much better than healing, because it saves the labour of being sick’ — appears in his collected Works. Even he, though, was reworking a commonplace far older than himself, and he did not write the trimmed modern wording that later sites pinned on Erasmus.

cite.sourceCitation: Adams, Thomas. “The Works of Thomas Adams.” London, 1630 (“prevention is so much better than healing…”). The five-word proverb is an anonymous English saying; no source ties the wording to Erasmus.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A five-word proverb got welded to a famous Renaissance name. Here is what the wording actually is — and is not.

items.why: The Dutch humanist wrote in Latin and died in 1536; the English sentence appears in none of his works, and his Adagia is a compilation of others’ classical proverbs, not his own coinages. The scholarly tracer WIST ↗ files the line under him only as “(Attributed),” and quote sites give no citation at all.

“Prevention is better than cure” is an English proverbial saying. Its earliest documented English form — “prevention is so much better than healing” — is in the sermons of Thomas Adams (1630), and the modern phrasing spread through the 1800s, per the Phrase Finder ↗.
The thought is ancient — the Roman satirist Persius (c. AD 58) urged meeting ‘the malady on its way,’ and versions run back through Chinese medicine, as a long history of the phrase ↗ sets out.

misattribution.truthLine: “Prevention is better than cure” is an old English proverb with no single author; the earliest documented English wording sits in the sermons of Thomas Adams ↗ (1630), and nothing ties it to Erasmus.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Few sayings feel as self-evidently wise as “prevention is better than cure” — which is exactly why it drifts toward a prestigious name. Erasmus, the great humanist compiler of proverbs, is a natural magnet: if anyone should have said it, surely he did. But wanting a line to be his is not evidence that it is.

The reality is more ordinary and more interesting. The concept is one of the oldest in medicine and law, voiced across centuries and continents; the specific English proverb is anonymous, sharpened over time by preachers and satirists rather than coined by one author. The Erasmus label is a modern quote-database habit, not a citation.
context.pull: If anyone should have said it, surely he did — but wanting a line to be his is not evidence.
